# IELTS Task 1 General Training — formal-letter demonstration (2026)

**Source:** IELTS Advantage, [IELTS Task 1 General Training Writing: Ultimate Guide 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZwTX-O_WvnM), 17 m 45 s.  
**Transcript:** complete auto-generated English captions exported and reviewed (280 lines). The video demonstrates one formal-letter prompt and ends by directing viewers to a separate informal-letter lesson. Treat this as a formal-letter walkthrough, not the complete General Training Task 1 course.

## The first decision: purpose, reader, and register

The prompt gives a situation, a recipient, three bullet points, and often an opening line. Read all of it before drafting. Decide what the letter must accomplish and address every bullet point adequately.

The video uses a two-way shortcut: a letter to a friend is “informal”; any other recipient is “formal.” **That binary is incomplete.** IELTS describes General Training letters as personal, semi-formal, or formal. A manager, teacher, landlord, or other person the writer knows may call for a semi-formal tone depending on the relationship and purpose. Choose register from the full context, then keep it consistent. ([IELTS General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing); [IELTS Task 1 writing preparation](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources))

The video teaches a “friend / not friend” rule and says there is no semi-formal category; do not teach that claim. Likewise, no fixed ban on contractions, phrasal verbs, or idiomatic wording works for all letter types. Avoid slang, texting abbreviations, and emojis; select wording and greeting/sign-off that suit the recipient and the task.

## Plan and organize the letter — 0:34–4:21

Use a quick outline before writing:

1. Follow the prompt’s requested opening when it supplies one (the example begins “Dear Sir or Madam”).
2. State the reason for writing near the start so the purpose is clear.
3. Give each of the three bullet points its own paragraph or otherwise make each one easy to identify. Add relevant detail to develop each function.
4. End the letter clearly with a register-appropriate sign-off and name. The lesson uses “Kind regards”; select a closing that fits the audience and the greeting.

The worked prompt asks the writer to review a moving company, describe good service, name a staff member who helped, and mention a problem. The learner’s plan turns each bullet into a clear response. The teacher suggests around 50 words for each bullet-point paragraph as a rough way to reach the 150-word minimum without counting every word. That is a planning aid, not a required allocation. A bullet may need more or less development; all three must be covered adequately.

IELTS requires at least 150 words. Task 1 takes about 20 minutes, and Task 2 contributes twice as much to the Writing score. The video’s advice to write Task 2 first is one possible timing strategy, not an official sequence. Practise an order that reliably leaves enough time for both tasks. Do not copy its older paper answer-sheet example without checking the current local interface.

## Develop relevant content — 4:21–7:35

Choose details that directly answer the bullet and that you can explain clearly. A personal memory, a plausible invented detail, or a simple example can work if it serves the task. The teacher tells the learner not to get stuck inventing names or impressive events; ordinary relevant content is enough. Do not add complex details that are hard to express accurately.

Keep the question visible while drafting. The teacher reviews each paragraph against the bullet it is meant to address, correcting the learner when a possible point has been postponed to an unnecessary conclusion. The letter needs a closing, but it does not need an essay-style conclusion that repeats the whole message.

## Formal wording and editing demonstration — 6:25–17:05

The formal-letter demonstration focuses on register and readability:

- avoid slang and text-message forms such as abbreviations or emojis;
- use a suitable greeting and sign-off;
- make paragraph breaks visible;
- state one or two connected ideas per sentence;
- use a full stop when one idea is complete rather than joining many clauses into a run-on sentence;
- check capitalization, apostrophes, punctuation, spelling, and whether a reader can tell where a sentence ends.

The teacher revises the learner’s long sentences into shorter, clearer ones, adds a paragraph break, and distinguishes a topic sentence from supporting explanation. Repeated issues in the sample include comma/full-stop confusion, an unclear full stop, capitalization after a comma, and a run-on sentence. The teaching point is careful editing for legibility and control, not a universal ban on complex sentences.

The example student’s earlier score and the video’s predicted improvement are not independently verified. Use the observed edits as examples of errors to check, not as proof of a guaranteed band increase.

## Reusable practice routine

1. Read the situation, recipient, purpose, and all three bullet points.
2. Label the appropriate register as personal, semi-formal, or formal; note a greeting and closing that match it.
3. Write a one-line purpose and a short point for each bullet.
4. Add relevant supporting detail that can be expressed accurately.
5. Draft with clear paragraphs and connected prose; do not use bullet points in the final letter.
6. Review coverage of all bullets, consistency of tone, purpose, paragraph breaks, sentence boundaries, punctuation, grammar, and the minimum word count.
7. Repeat under the approximate 20-minute limit and examine feedback against Task Achievement and language control.

## Official cross-checks

- [IELTS General Training Writing format](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-general-training-test/ielts-general-training-format-writing): Task 1 is a letter of at least 150 words; style can be personal, semi-formal, or formal; the recipient and relationship guide the tone; Task 2 is weighted twice as much.
- [IELTS Writing preparation resources](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/preparation-resources/writing-test-resources): purpose, consistent register, appropriate letter format, and full coverage of the task bullets.
- [IELTS Writing key assessment criteria](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-writing-key-assessment-criteria.pdf): Task Achievement includes clear purpose, coverage and appropriate development of all three bullet-point functions, suitable format, and consistent tone.
